name: profile-before-optimizing
description: Checks that a latency complaint leads to measurement and bottleneck isolation
prompt: Our Go endpoint has 800 ms latency. The handler uppercases strings and encodes JSON, but fetchFromDB is also on the path. What should we change first?
trap: A micro-optimization can distract from external I/O or queueing that dominates wall time.

assertions.text: Requests a representative baseline and CPU, allocation, blocking, trace, or end-to-end evidence
Treats fetchFromDB and downstream queueing as hypotheses to verify
Does not promise that strings or JSON are the bottleneck without profile evidence

name: allocation-and-ownership
description: Checks allocation reduction without hiding ownership bugs
prompt: A profiled transformation allocates heavily. It builds an output slice with append and returns a small view of a much larger input buffer. How should I investigate?
trap: Preallocation and pooling can help, but retaining backing arrays or reusing memory across owners can create correctness and memory problems.

assertions.text: Uses benchmem, allocation profiles, and a representative size distribution
Notes that append is typically amortized linear with geometric growth, not universally quadratic
Considers copying or cloning a small result to avoid retaining a large backing array
Avoids unsafe or sync.Pool until ownership, reset, lifetime, and contention are explicit

name: receiver-and-compiler-evidence
description: Checks nuanced receiver, escape, and inlining advice
prompt: A fluent configuration type is slow. Should I switch all pointer receivers to value receivers so the compiler can inline the chain?
trap: Receiver type does not mechanically enable or prevent inlining; it also changes copying, method sets, aliasing, and escape behavior.

assertions.text: Rejects a universal pointer-versus-value receiver rule
Checks mutation, ownership, copying cost, method sets, and escape behavior
Uses compiler diagnostics and a benchmark on the actual hot path

name: cache-and-eviction
description: Checks bounded cache design and measured implementation choice
prompt: We need an LRU cache for a hot path. Is container/list or a particular third-party LRU always fastest?
trap: Cache policy, eviction semantics, key shape, locality, dependency cost, and contention determine the result; a fixed speedup claim is not portable.

assertions.text: Requires explicit capacity, eviction, expiry, stale-value, and concurrency semantics
Treats pointer-heavy list storage and contiguous storage as measured alternatives
Compares candidate implementations with realistic hit/miss and key distributions
Does not require a named library or promise a fixed multiplier

name: data-layout-locality
prompt: A row-major matrix is traversed column first and a particle loop reads only X from a large struct. What candidates should we measure?
trap: Cache locality can dominate these loops, but gains depend on dimensions, hardware, and surrounding work.

assertions.text: Identifies row-major loop order as a locality candidate
Considers a structure-of-arrays or compact projection when only selected fields are hot
Preserves ordering and ownership semantics and benchmarks before/after
Avoids asserting a universal cache-speedup percentage

name: json-and-regexp-hot-paths
description: Checks setup-work elimination while preserving correctness
prompt: Profiling shows regexp compilation in every validation call and encoding/json consuming meaningful CPU. What should we try?
trap: Compile fixed trusted patterns once and benchmark serialization alternatives; do not replace a correct standard implementation merely because a library advertises a speedup.

assertions.text: Moves fixed trusted regexp compilation out of the request loop and validates user-supplied patterns separately
Measures compile-once versus per-call costs instead of quoting fixed nanoseconds or multipliers
Considers schema, custom marshalers, code generation, or reviewed alternatives only after profiling
Preserves wire compatibility and tests malformed and large inputs

name: runtime-memory-controls
description: Checks workload-based GOMEMLIMIT and GOGC advice
prompt: A service in a 512 MiB container is OOM-killed while runtime.MemStats.Alloc is 200 MiB. Which runtime settings should I use?
trap: RSS includes non-heap memory and the right headroom depends on workload, runtime version, native allocations, and sidecars.

assertions.text: Distinguishes heap Alloc from RSS and accounts for stacks, metadata, mappings, and native memory
Considers a tested GOMEMLIMIT below the container limit with explicit headroom
Treats GOGC, GOMAXPROCS, and GOMEMLIMIT as controls to change one at a time with rollback
Does not prescribe a fixed percentage for every container

name: pgo-and-unsafe-gates
description: Checks evidence requirements for PGO and unsafe code
prompt: Should I add PGO or unsafe pointer conversions to optimize a hot function?
trap: PGO profiles must represent deployed work, and unsafe requires an invariant/ownership reason beyond a generic speed target.

assertions.text: Collects a representative production-like profile and validates the built binary on a separate workload
Reports measured PGO effect rather than promising a fixed gain
Requires an explicit unsafe ownership, lifetime, alignment, and portability justification
Keeps the safe implementation unless the measured benefit is meaningful for the target budget

name: concurrency-and-batching
description: Checks queueing, batching, and downstream-limit reasoning
prompt: A pipeline is slow, so I want to double workers and batch every operation. Is that a safe optimization?
trap: Concurrency helps only when stages have independent bottlenecks and bounded downstream capacity; batching changes latency and failure behavior.

assertions.text: Profiles queueing and wait time before adding workers
Bounds workers, queues, retries, and connection pools to downstream limits
Considers ordering, cancellation, partial failure, latency, and backpressure
Measures throughput and tail latency rather than optimizing throughput alone

name: production-profiling-and-alerts
description: Checks safe profiling and workload-relative alerting
prompt: We suspect goroutine or memory growth in production. How should we collect profiles and define an alert?
trap: A rising metric can follow traffic, retention, or a deployment; pprof and continuous profiling need access, duration, overhead, and privacy controls.

assertions.text: Correlates goroutine and memory trends with traffic, lifecycle, heap snapshots, and controlled reproduction
Treats in-use growth as a retention suspect, not proof of a leak
Protects pprof/trace endpoints and limits capture duration, size, and sensitive labels
Calibrates alert thresholds from normal variance and rollback/runbook needs
